title: The Heart of Zen
speaker: Ryushin Andrea Thach
summary: Ryushin Andrea Thach takes up an untitled poem by Jane Hirshfield, "You must try, the voice said, to become colder," which Ryushin first heard in a talk by dharma sister Mary Mocine. Colder comes to mean receiving pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral feeling equally, as when Ryushin sat in sesshin between a dear friend and a disliked man and let the body be both hot and cold. A man who leaps onto the subway tracks to shield a stranger from an oncoming train and says only "I just did it" shows what the poem's heartlessness looks like. In the closing questions, a participant asks about people who lack that automatic kindness, and Ryushin answers that the seeds of wholeness are present in everyone.

sentences.text: Good evening everyone.
The title of this talk is "Something Like the Heart of Zen."
Like most things, it arises out of a theme I've been working on.
I was listening to a talk that my teacher gave recently, and at some point he says in it, "If a teacher is not making his students uncomfortable, he's not teaching."
That's what the story I'm going to tell tonight reminds me of.
It's a poem that was given as a talk by one of my dharma sisters, Mary Mocine, so many years ago.
The poem landed right between my eyes.
It made me very uncomfortable because it hit something really deep and confusing for me.
I've been working with it ever since, and this is where I am with it right now.
In these recent many months, like many of us, I've been working with having strong emotions.
I've been aware of how I'm a very affective person.
I have emotions very readily.
I've always been one of those people who are sensitive.
I've thought that in some ways that's not so bad, because when I feel something deeply, when I'm moved by a situation, tears arise very readily.
Then I wondered about that.
I wondered what that really was for me, and this poem came to mind.
It's a poem by Jane Hirschfield, who is a longtime Zen student and a really wonderful poet, if you don't know her poetry.
I don't know if it has a title.
It's very short.
It goes:
*You must try, the voice said, to become colder.
I understood it once.
It's like the bodies of gods cast in bronze and braced in stone.
Only something heartless could bear the full weight.*
Let me read that one more time.
*You must try, the voice said, to become colder.
I understood it once.
It's like the bodies of gods cast in bronze, braced in stone.
Only something heartless could bear the full weight.*
Now, I understood this poem in one way at the time, and it was reasonable medicine for me, but I'm going to try and unpack it in a little different way.
It's kind of stark, isn't it?
It strips you bare, and you wonder, what am I left with?
Especially with this group.
I think of this group as people who especially understand the warmth of Zen, not the coldness of Zen, which Zen is sometimes accused of.
But this says, get colder, become heartless.
So the voice of this poem initially is a voice that comes from outside.
"You must try," the voice said.
Is that our better self?
Is that the person who knows?
Is that the parent who knows?
Is that the super ego that knows that somehow we have to change directions, that what we're doing is off base?
Is it a voice of wisdom that knows?
But we're being talked to.
That voice is not coming from within ourselves initially in this poem.
"You must try," the voice said, "to become colder."
Colder sounds pretty aversive.
Who wants to be cold?
Who wants to be cold around here?
Give me another layer, would you please?
Who wants to be hot either?
I could stand to get out of some of these layers right now.
But actually in Zen, either one of those things is a problem, getting hotter or getting colder.
They're both a problem.
I remember sitting in one sesshin.
I hope I haven't told this story here before.
It seems I told it not long ago.
I was sitting in a sesshin many years ago, and I remember where I was on the tan, the raised platform in the zendo, in my home temple.
On one side of me was a person I liked very, very much.
I had such a warm feeling for this person.
He had been very close to my teacher, my first teacher who had died.
I really enjoyed Howard very much.
On the other side was someone I really didn't like at all.
I didn't like being anywhere near him, actually.
Somehow I got seated right between these two people.
I felt hot and I felt cold.
It was very uncomfortable.
Then I thought to myself, why don't I just be hot and cold?
I allowed the sensations, really in my mind, my very strong mind back then, to be both hot and cold.
In between, both of them were just fine.
There was neither a strong leaning towards nor a strong pushing away.
I think this is the colder that's being pointed at.
No matter what we do, we're grasping for something.
Even if we're pushing away, we're actually grasping for something else.
So if we're colder, we're actually approaching with a mind that wants neither, in a certain way.
Let me, I have this idea also that emotions are more valuable.
Do you have this feeling for yourself, that somehow emotions are more me?
They're like the core of what I'm about.
Maybe that's not true for everyone.
Some people may think it's their ideas, their sense of what they bring to the world.
I think, therefore I am.
But I think actually most of us feel like, I feel, therefore I am.
Whatever that place is that we live in.
The women in the room are nodding at me.
I don't know if everyone is nodding at me or not.
But actually in basic Buddhist psychology, our ideas and our emotions are all of one thing.
This is very interesting to me.
When I went back to reread this to prepare for the talk, I went, oh yeah, that's right.
My feelings of liking something, of anger, of irritation, of warmth, of love, of kindness, of all of that, that's also a formation when it arises out of a place that's about me.
Not from the kind of big self, but from my ordinary self.
Just like ideas arise in that way.
Our ideas and our emotions arise in the same way.
They're colored by our experiences, some conscious, some unconscious, of who we are.
And the twelve-fold wheel of causation, I promise not to bore you all with this too much, is the way in which our thinking arises and we become someone or something.
It's really basic Buddhism.
It was the first of the Buddha's great insights in the night, actually it was the last of the Buddha's great insights on the night of his awakening.
We see the way in which our ignorance gives rise to the idea that things are a certain thing.
We receive it through our sense organs.
We have contact with that object.
We imagine it to be something that's completely outside of ourselves.
Feelings arrive, then the cravings: I like, I don't like, I want, I don't want.
We start to cling, push away, or grab onto, and we become a certain person who behaves in a certain way.

One of the key turning points to unlock the twelve-fold wheel of causation is what's meant by feelings in Buddhist psychology, and that is simply the recognition of something as being pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral.
There's no idea of good or bad in here.
There's no idea of want or not want.
That comes later, and that's completely conditioned by our ideas about things.
Oh, that smells bad to me.
That smells good.
That tastes good.
That's terrible.
That reminds me of my mom's terrific souffle.
I wish I could have some of that right now.
That's all down the line, but just pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral, that's the true feeling realm, and that of itself has no value or valence to it.
It's the colder that Jane Hirschfield is pointing at.
The "get colder" is the part before it's colored, before it's fleshed in by this self.
You must try to get colder.
You must try.
We have such a negative idea about objective.
I would say it's to take it all in, to take it all in equally, to receive it all equally.
You must try to receive it all equally.
"I understood it once."
You know when you have that experience of just, I like him, I don't like him, well, let me just take it all in at once.
Equal.
Right here in this seat in the middle.
Equal.
I understood at once.
When you receive and experience life in that way, you say, ah, yes, that's it.
You've all had that experience of just getting circumstances as they are and receiving them, and you feel this release, this relief in that moment.
"I understood it once."
It's no longer the voice outside, but my own reality.
Oh, this is how it is.
This is how it is.
"It's like the bodies of gods."
You know, in Greek mythology, gods were the people who sat up on Mount Olympus and pulled all the strings and controlled everything, right?
They knew how it all worked, and they were above this terrible human existence that we live in.
But actually the gods are cast in bronze and braced in stone.
They have to in some way protect themselves, cover themselves in precious material or be made out of full stone in order to bear the full weight.
The gods are like we are, of a human existence.
There's no becoming completely separate from it.
Even they must be cast and braced.
You can think about it like the story of the Zen master whose child dies and he breaks down sobbing, and his students run up to him and say, what's wrong?
I thought you were actualized.
I thought you understood about life and death.
And the teacher says, "I do.
That's why I'm crying."
It's like that.
"Only something heartless."
Only something heartless.
Oh, isn't that just so distasteful?
How can we spend so much of our life wanting to express our heart, wanting to be hearted?
That's how we usually think about heartedness.
I looked this up.
There are at least seventy different ways we talk about expressing heartedness.
There are a few of them.
Some of them point to a positive attribute: a big heart, a heart of gold, all heart.
Close, near, dear to one's heart.
Cross my heart.
Follow my heart.
Another is that we aspire to be in that position: from the heart.
The heart is in the right place.
We reference it as sincere action: bare one's heart.
My heart goes out to, from the bottom of my heart.
My heart bleeds for.
To take something to heart.
Lacking it can be a problem: a heart of stone.
Didn't have the heart.
Faint of heart.
Not know one's heart.
One's heart sinks.
To be sick at heart.
Or it can be an impediment: a bleeding heart, to nearly give one a heart attack.
There are all kinds of ways of being hearted and heartless.
That's usually how we think about being hearted.
That's normally how we think about our emotions.
But our heart is not, as we were saying, our ideas or our opinions.
It's not what we think of ourselves as being.

Some years ago in shosan, which is a ceremony some of you may not have been at, where the teacher sits usually after the end of a period of some days of meditation, everyone's very concentrated and very intimate and connected.
People are seated like this, and each person comes to the end of the mat and comes and bows to the teacher and asks a very sincere question.

In one year, one of the students who had been studying for many, many years, a woman who had a lot of heart and wore her heart on her sleeve and cared very much about things, came up and bowed and asked what to do with all of her emotions.
And the teacher said, "Throw your heart away.
Throw that part of you that feels like it has to feel deeply and connect with everything and wear your heart on your sleeve.
Throw it away.
Get colder."
What's Buddha's heart?

It's not that it doesn't cry when it's alone or doesn't scream or ache or call out at the thought of the innocence being gassed in Syria or the incarcerated in prisons, or well up with tears at the reunion of a family that's been separated or the sight of kindness.
That's not what Buddha's heart is.
Buddha's heart is that which holds everything together.
When you throw away your heart, what remains?
When you throw away your personal heart, what's underneath it all?
I think it resides in a place that understands deeply what our connectedness is.
I think it transcends our usual way of living our lives.

You might say there's a theory these days that it resides in the mirror neurons and that sense of limbic resonance that understands deeply what the experience is of another person and takes that as oneself.
The idea is that these neurons in our brain are activated when one sees the same action performed by another.
Perhaps their action is like the call of one animal responding to the call of its mate.
Some argue that this is the source of our true empathy.
Perhaps that's the heartlessness, the heartedness of heartlessness.
Remember when this theory was first being put out?
Maybe some of you read the articles too.
There's a story in New York City of the subway line.
Do you remember this?
A man had a seizure and fell off the platform at the subway in front of an oncoming train.
And another man who was standing on the platform with his two young daughters, the train arriving, leaves them.
He jumps off the platform in front of this train to rescue the man, and there was no time to pull him up.
What did he do but land and cover him up?
They both lay right underneath, in the middle part in between the tracks, so that the subway went over them.
Neither one of them was hurt.
The little girls are crying.
Their dad jumped in front of the train.
Everyone attends to them, and he rescued the man.
People came up to him: "What were you thinking, you great hero?
How did this happen?
How did you respond?"
He said, "I don't know.
I just did it.
I don't know.
I just did it."
That's how we act this way.
I think he threw his heart away.
He didn't think about the girls.
He didn't think about himself.
He just saw what needed to be done and he knew how to do it.
Now the theory is that we learn how to do this, how to act out of the heartless heartedness, because we see other people do it.
We recognize something.
It resonates with us.
Perhaps it was his mother over and over again, and how she tended to him or to the neighbors or was kind.
Maybe it was the father or a teacher or a friend who had done that many times before, and so he just knew what it was that he had to do without ever being told or ever having done it before.
That's how we do it.
That's why we sit zazen.
That's why we practice with each other over and over again.
We find that place.
We see that place in each other as we manifest.
We learn to recognize it, to know it without even being conscious about it.
I think perhaps that's the strength of the gods, bronze and cast.
It's their strength to just throw it all away, their ideas of themselves.
What does it mean to bear the full weight?
Well, what is that weight?
When I first heard this poem I thought about all the suffering in life, all the things that were difficult.
They certainly were difficult for me, and I felt like there was a lot that I had to bear all the time, and maybe I just had to get colder so I didn't feel it so much.
But actually now I understand this in a very different kind of way.
What is that weight?
You see, Buddhism really isn't about suffering.
That's a little known secret.
People hear the first noble truth and they want out the door.
The first noble truth is there is suffering.
But actually another version of that is that there is nirvana.
Everything is included.
Everything is included.
It's all about our lives and living our lives.
Buddhism is all about our lives and living our lives.
It's the whole package.
What if we could see it clearly, understand it clearly?
What would this weight be then?
What would it be if we weren't in the center of it?
What if we actually took our proper place, which was part of the whole working of the universe?
What if we could really understand that we're completely supported by everything in a way that's so awesome that it's a terrible weight to bear, isn't it?
Can you really imagine that you're that big, that important, that supported, that loved, that cared for by the whole universe?
But what would it mean if you were also responsible for everyone and everything?
That's the other side of it, of course, because we are.
If we're supported by everything and everything supports us, then that means that we have a role in everything else.
Is that the terrible weight that we have to bear?
Maybe it is.
How can you possibly wrap your mind around that?
Only a god, only something that was heartless in the sense of recognizing that it's so much bigger.
This life is so much bigger than my own pains and fears and difficulties and joys.
It's all contained in one, you see.
That doesn't mean that we don't feel pain and loss and difficulty, but when we recognize at times that it's actually part of this big working of things, somehow it's different.
*You must try, the voice said, to be colder.*
I understood it once.

When you have those moments, like the Buddha as a small child sitting under the rose apple tree, recognizing everything is just right in the world as it is, and you have that moment of awakening, you understand that it's okay to be heartless.
The whole weight is born.
I think that's what I wanted to say.
I don't know if that made any sense at all or not, and I don't know what time it is.
We have a time for a thought or a response from one or two of you.
Yeah, Talus?
**Participant:** It feels like one of the important aspects of this teaching is stepping outside of dualism, like much of the koans.
For example, you helped me uncover that trying to be colder is not exclusive of being one.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** That's right.
You can still have a heart.
Thank you.
John?
**Participant:** With the being colder, I thought about what helps you face a particular situation, and sometimes being colder helps.
If someone is bleeding, you need to be able to face that and help them instead of, like, "Oh, I don't like blood."
There are times when coldness helps a person engage and do what needs to be done.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** It's a wonderful example.
It's like jumping off the subway.
If he had stopped and thought about, "Will his children be frightened while I get killed?"
Well, he wouldn't have ever jumped.
**Participant:** Yeah.
I just read a quote from Rosa Parks.
She said, "When you know what needs to be done, there is no fear."
It's a nice thing to be fortunate enough to know what needs to be done and not be too confused.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Very related.
Yeah.
Thank you.
Anyone else?
**Participant:** Just thinking about what's beneath that heart.
You mentioned that if the parents were nurturing in a way, like that man, perhaps that gave him this automatic response to help.
But what about people that don't have that automatic response?
Maybe the best teaching for them isn't to be colder, but to be warmer.
But I understand the teaching that Talus was [unclear: "with the learning team"] as well, that we want to include everything.
But you were suggesting a kind of trust and surrender that can happen when you throw the heart away.
But what about the automatic responses that lead to acting out of fear or violence in the absence of heart?
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** Thank you.
I'm tired enough that I may not be tracking your question well enough, so excuse me if I'm missing you.
I'm trying to point towards a kind of colder that isn't cold, but is more, if you will, equanimous, more even in the circumstance.
So it's neither one set of emotion we might describe as being very affective and open, nor one that is very closed, but one that receives everything.
Does that help?
**Participant:** It does.
But you were also speaking to an automatic response that this man had.
And I wonder, if someone isn't thinking, are they necessarily going to act out of kindness?
But maybe that's beside the point a little bit.
**Ryushin Andrea Thach:** It might be.
But just to say what Buddhism would say: the seeds of wholeness, wholeness meaning the untainted, unharmed wholeness that we all have, is present in everyone.

Some people have more circumstances, whether they've sat a whole lot more zazen or whether they had a nurturing environment, or they just have a somewhat different psychology that sets them in a way that orients more that way.
And there are others that have very negative experiences, that have a lot to overcome to be able to access that part of themselves.
Not everyone jumped off the platform.
Okay, well, I think that's probably what we have for tonight.
Thank you very much for your attention.
